items.why: Clearly distinguishes the festival meal, when they cursed Abimelek, from the earlier grape work.
The stem awkwardly treats the curse as occurring after the punishment even though it appears to constitute that punishment.
Strong sequence-and-agent distinction: the five men take the objects before the priest later carries them along.
Precisely contrasts the five spies who enter and take the objects with those standing at the gate.
The passage directly identifies fear of Abimelek, not fear of Shechem’s citizens, as Jotham’s reason.
Strongly distinguishes the relatives entrusted with the message from the citizens who are to receive it.
Resolving “him” requires distinguishing Jerub-Baal from the nearby mention of Abimelek.
The competitor nearly restates the same movement, since going to the fields entails coming out of the city.
The shouting is the immediate trigger for turning, whereas overtaking occurred before it.
The doorway approach has the specific purpose of setting the tower on fire, beyond the broader ongoing attack.
The route resolves the answer, though the stem’s repeated wording about the residence is cumbersome.
The sequence is recoverable, but calling the conditional blessing a “request” is unnatural.
It cleanly separates the stated causal reason—lack of an inheritance—from the incidental absence of a king.
Strongly distinguishes the priests’ service until captivity from the idol’s use while God’s house was at Shiloh.
The fire plainly causes the deaths, while entering the stronghold merely places the occupants there.
The covert sender is clearly Zebul, while Gaal is the person whose actions he reports.
Grammar assigns the request to the trees; gods and humans are only those cheered by the vine’s wine.
The olive tree’s rhetorical question clearly gives preserving its oil as the reason for refusing rule.
The causal reading is clear, but this nearly duplicates the stronger olive-tree refusal item.
The abstract phrase “does something” merely asks the reader to translate the pronoun “him” back into a name.
Micah explicitly bases his expectation on having the Levite as priest, not on the Levite’s hometown.
It tests Zebul’s reinterpretation of the apparent people as mountain shadows, though the stem is slightly clunky.
The passage explicitly links prosperity to a land lacking nothing; the Sidonian comparison concerns security.
The servant’s action has a clear object, requiring a basic but useful distinction between killer and victim.
Jotham states that listening to him is meant to result in God listening to the citizens.
Strongly distinguishes the Levite’s purpose in leaving from Micah’s house, which is only his eventual destination.
The embedded report assigns the curse to Micah’s mother even though Micah is the current speaker.
It distinguishes why rescue was unavailable—distance and isolation—from why rescue was needed.
The pronoun in “take it over” refers to the land, while the people are the proposed targets of attack.
Excellent distinction between whom the mother says will make the image and the silversmith who actually makes it.
Clearly separates the priest whom they ask from God, the source from whom the priest is to seek guidance.
